lessons.title: Position Sizing and Risk Controls for an ML-Driven Strategy

children.text: Chapter 1's case study promised three fixes for its 87%-accurate model that still lost money: confidence-based position sizing, volatility-based position sizing, and a max-loss-per-trade rule. This lesson builds all three properly, and adds a fourth layer, a portfolio-level circuit breaker, that none of the earlier lessons named yet. Together, these four layers are what actually turn a validated signal, from Chapter 3, into something safe enough to trade.

body.text: Position sizing and risk controls are not an afterthought bolted onto a good model. They are the layer that decides whether a real predictive edge survives contact with the market's occasional worst days, exactly the layer Chapter 1's case study skipped entirely by using the same fixed position size on every single trade.

children.text: Lesson 2 introduced the confidence threshold, only acting on predictions the model feels strongly enough about. Confidence-based sizing goes one step further: among the trades that clear the threshold, size scales with how far the model's predicted probability sits from the 50-50 midpoint, treating a 58% probability as a smaller conviction than a 72% one, rather than trading both identically. A simple version scales linearly between the threshold and a chosen cap, giving a modest size to a signal that barely clears the bar and a full size to one the model is genuinely confident about.

body.caption: A simple confidence-based position size multiplier

markDefs.definition: A position sizing method that sizes each trade so its expected rupee risk matches a fixed target, using current market volatility, rather than trading a fixed quantity regardless of conditions.

children.text: Instead of a fixed number of shares or lots,

sizes each trade so its expected rupee movement stays close to a fixed target risk amount, using the realized volatility feature built back in Lesson 6 and used as a target in Lesson 7. On calm days, lower volatility means the same target risk buys a larger position. On turbulent days, the identical formula automatically shrinks it, without anyone needing to notice the turbulence and intervene manually.

body.caption: Sizing to a fixed rupee risk target instead of a fixed quantity
body.code:
import numpy as np

target_risk_per_trade = 5_000                        # rupees you're willing to have at stake per trade
daily_vol = df["realized_vol_20d"] / np.sqrt(252)    # de-annualize the Lesson 6/7 volatility feature

position_value = target_risk_per_trade / daily_vol
# on calm days (low daily_vol), this allows a larger position;
# on turbulent days (high daily_vol), the same formula automatically shrinks it

children.text: Max-Loss-Per-Trade: A Hard Backstop, Not a Suggestion

Both sizing rules above only act before a trade is placed, using what is already known: the model's confidence, and recent volatility. Neither can anticipate a genuinely unprecedented move that exceeds what recent history suggested was likely, exactly the kind of tail event behind Chapter 1's -₹28,000 losing trades. A max-loss-per-trade rule, implemented as a stop-loss or a pre-committed exit price, caps the damage on any single trade regardless of how large the actual move turns out to be, or why it happened. It is the one layer in this lesson that does not depend on a forecast being right.
Portfolio-Level Circuit Breaker: When to Stop Trading Entirely

The first three layers manage risk trade by trade. A fourth layer manages risk at the level of the whole strategy: a rule that reduces or halts all trading once the strategy's own drawdown, the metric introduced in Lesson 13, exceeds a pre-set threshold. A string of losses can mean bad luck within an otherwise sound strategy, or it can mean the model's edge has genuinely broken down, a regime shift, in Lesson 11's terms. A portfolio-level circuit breaker does not need to know which explanation is true. It simply stops a manageable drawdown from becoming an account-ending one while the question gets investigated properly.

body.text: No single layer here is sufficient alone. Confidence-based sizing does nothing if a low-volatility day suddenly turns violent. Volatility-based sizing does nothing about a low-conviction signal traded at full size. A per-trade stop does nothing to catch a slow, grinding string of small losses across many trades. The four layers work together precisely because each one catches a failure mode the others miss.

columns.label: Trade-Level Layers
points: Confidence-based sizing: protects against trading weak, near-random signals at full size
Volatility-based sizing: protects against taking normal-sized risk on abnormally turbulent days
Max-loss-per-trade: protects against a single trade moving far beyond what any sizing formula anticipated

columns.label: Strategy-Level Layer
points: Portfolio-level circuit breaker: protects against continuing to trade at full size through a genuine breakdown in the model's edge
Triggers on the strategy's own drawdown, from Lesson 13
Buys time to investigate whether a losing streak is bad luck or a real regime shift
A structured, more formal sizing framework, the Kelly criterion, is covered in its own dedicated course on this platform for readers who want to go further

body.title: Which layers apply here?
body.question: A model's predicted probability for a trade is 0.58, just above a 0.55 confidence threshold. Recent market volatility is also unusually high. Which two of this lesson's tools would work together to correctly size this specific trade smaller than a typical trade?
options: Confidence-based sizing only, since volatility does not matter for position sizing
Confidence-based sizing, because 0.58 is close to the threshold, and volatility-based sizing, because current volatility is elevated
Only the portfolio-level circuit breaker applies to a single trade like this
Max-loss-per-trade, because it is the only tool that adjusts position size before a trade
body.explanation: Both trade-level sizing tools apply here and reinforce each other: confidence-based sizing shrinks the position because 0.58 is only barely above the threshold, and volatility-based sizing independently shrinks it further because current market turbulence is high. The max-loss-per-trade rule and the portfolio circuit breaker are backstops, not sizing formulas, they act after a position is already on.

body.title: Choosing a max-loss level
body.scenario: A trader's volatility-based sizing formula, on a calm day, allocates a position worth ₹2,00,000 to a single Nifty options trade. He has not yet set a max-loss-per-trade rule.
body.prompt: Why is a max-loss-per-trade rule still necessary even though volatility-based sizing already adjusted this position for current conditions?
body.modelAnswer: Volatility-based sizing adjusts position size using recent, already-observed volatility, but it cannot anticipate a sudden, unprecedented move that exceeds what recent history suggested was likely, exactly the kind of tail event behind Chapter 1's case study losses. A max-loss-per-trade rule acts as a hard backstop that does not depend on any volatility forecast at all, it simply caps the damage once a trade has already moved further against the position than the trader is willing to accept, regardless of why that move happened or whether any sizing formula predicted it.

body.title: Position Sizing and Risk Controls: Core Terms

cards.definition: Scaling a trade's position size based on how far the model's predicted probability sits from the 50-50 midpoint, giving stronger convictions larger positions.
A position sizing method that sizes each trade so its expected rupee risk matches a fixed target, using current market volatility, rather than trading a fixed quantity regardless of conditions.
A risk control that caps how much a single trade can lose, regardless of how large the underlying market move turns out to be.
A rule that reduces or halts all trading once a strategy's own drawdown exceeds a pre-set threshold, protecting against a genuine breakdown in the strategy's edge.
A formal mathematical framework for sizing bets based on estimated edge and odds, known for being aggressive if used at full strength; covered in depth in its own dedicated course.

points: Confidence-based sizing scales a trade's size with how strongly the model believes in it, rather than trading every signal that clears the threshold identically.
Volatility-based sizing targets a fixed rupee risk per trade using current market volatility, automatically shrinking positions on turbulent days without manual intervention.
A max-loss-per-trade rule is a hard backstop that caps a single trade's damage regardless of forecasts, catching exactly the kind of tail event that broke Chapter 1's case study.

A portfolio-level circuit breaker manages risk at the strategy level, reducing or halting trading once overall drawdown crosses a threshold, buying time to check whether a losing streak reflects a genuine regime shift.
These four layers work together because each one catches a different failure mode; no single layer alone is a substitute for the other three.
